channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Researchers identify genetic 'convergence' in autism and a possible explanation for the female protective effect
item.description: In many cases, all it takes is one mutated gene to orchestrate changes across a whole network of genes linked to autism, according to new results published in Nature by researchers at Boston Children's Hospital. The finding could explain why different mutations in one or several of the hundreds of genes linked to autism can lead to a similar condition.

item.title: Drawings of near-death experiences reveal patterns in what people remember seeing
item.description: For people who have near-death experiences (NDEs), these encounters can be so deeply moving and life-changing that language seems inadequate. Many describe them as vivid, multisensory experiences, filled with mental imagery of colors, places and people.

item.title: Lung antibodies can be measured in exhaled breath
item.description: For the first time, researchers have successfully measured antibodies against specific respiratory viruses in exhaled air. The new study, involving the Karolinska Institutet, was published in eBioMedicine. The method may make it easier to study the immune system in the small airways of the lungs.

item.title: Moderate drinking carries health risks even within UK alcohol guidelines
item.description: Alcohol is deeply embedded in British culture, from celebrations and religious ceremonies to everyday social life. Government guidelines offer a way to reduce the risks associated with drinking, but consuming alcohol within recommended limits does not mean those risks disappear.

item.title: Digital therapy offers new way to prevent worsening anxiety around childbirth
item.description: Pregnant women with undiagnosed anxiety could benefit from a new digital therapy, according to a clinical trial led by King's College London. Published in JAMA Network Open, the results from the REducing Levels of AnXiety (RELAX) study have shown that self-led digital therapy significantly reduced participants' pre- and post-birth anxiety compared with participants who received usual care.

item.title: Collapsible bicycle helmets provide less protection on average than conventional helmets, new study finds
item.description: New research from Imperial College London has found that, on average, collapsible (sometimes called "foldable") bicycle helmets provide lower levels of protection against serious head injuries than noncollapsible helmets.

item.title: Alternative pathways for blood vessel growth could become targets against drug-resistant tumors
item.description: Researchers at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC), together with international collaborators, have uncovered previously unknown mechanisms that allow blood vessels to grow even in the absence of VEGF–VEGFR2 signaling, one of the best-known and most widely targeted pathways in clinical efforts to block tumor angiogenesis, growth and metastasis.

item.title: Mother-infant bonding linked to brain connectivity before birth
item.description: Pregnancy is a period of change and adaptation, characterized by psychological and neurobiological changes associated with the transition to motherhood and the development of caregiving behaviors. One of the central aspects of this process is maternal-fetal attachment (MFA), the emotional bond between a pregnant woman and her unborn baby, reflected in her thoughts, feelings and behaviors toward the fetus.

item.title: Uncovering rules for aggressive brain tumors could lead to better treatments
item.description: Aggressive brain tumors follow predictable rules, not chaotic randomness, according to new research. This discovery could lead to new, much-needed ways to treat glioblastoma tumors in the future.

item.title: Mice that watch fights come away battle-ready
item.description: People love to watch violent things. From slasher films to boxing, there's some intrinsic appeal to watching people get pummeled. The dystopian thriller "Squid Game," for instance, debuted in 2021 and in three years racked up 330 million streams totaling more than 2.8 billion hours viewed. Even monkeys pay more attention to videos of other monkeys fighting.

item.title: Emergency surgery verification linked to lower death rates, shorter hospital stays
item.description: Patients treated at hospitals that earned American College of Surgeons (ACS) Emergency General Surgery Verification demonstrated lower 30-day death rates and experienced shorter hospital stays after their hospitals earned verification, according to an analysis published in JAMA Surgery. The analysis included more than 20,000 patients who underwent emergency general surgery at 55 hospitals, five of which became verified during the study period.

item.title: Pulse oximetry–based scoring may miss sleep apnea events in Black patients
item.description: Sleep studies often use a pulse oximeter to determine the severity of sleep apnea. But a new study by investigators from Mass General Brigham reports that pulse oximeters may undercount breathing events in Black patients, potentially leading to inaccurate severity classifications.

item.title: Prostate cancer drug shows promise in new clinical trial
item.description: In a recent Yale-led clinical trial, a new type of prostate cancer drug showed promising results in reducing tumor activity and pain for patients with metastatic prostate cancer.

item.title: Millions of Americans are driving while dangerously tired
item.description: More than 6 in 10 American drivers admit they've driven while dangerously sleepy.

item.title: Does time on social media make teens anxious and depressed? The evidence is not so clear
item.description: Parents are understandably worried about the impact of social media on the mental health of their children.

item.title: Extreme heat days may increase dementia risk, with poorer communities facing greater vulnerability
item.description: Over 57 million people worldwide are living with dementia, with nearly 10 million new cases diagnosed each year, and scientists now say that people living in certain climatic conditions are at a greater risk than others of developing this neurodegenerative condition.

item.title: Australia is set to get a Wegovy pill. How does it compare with weight‑loss injections?
item.description: A new tablet version of Wegovy, a peptide used to help people lose weight, has been approved for the first time in Australia.

item.title: AI uncovers rapid changes in Parkinson's brain signals by separating rhythms from background activity
item.description: A research team led by professor Ji-Woong Choi of the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at DGIST has developed NONOS, a deep learning–based analysis technology that precisely separates rhythms from the underlying background signals in brain signals with high temporal resolution. The team collaborated with research teams led by professor Han-Joon Kim of Kumoh National Institute of Technology, professor Kyong Hwan Jin of Korea University and Dr. Jong-Cheol Rah of the Korea Brain Research Institute. The findings are published in NeuroImage.

item.title: Hydrogel could be potential treatment for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
item.description: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects approximately 38% of the global population, with prevalence continuing to rise in parallel with the global burden of metabolic syndrome. Although several pharmacological agents are currently under clinical investigation, approved therapeutic options remain limited in both efficacy and scope.

item.title: A much-needed new way to inactivate GPCRs, the most common drug targets
item.description: About one-third of all drugs approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration target G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a family of more than 800 cell-surface receptors that regulate a wide range of vital functions, including blood pressure, heart rate and immunity.

item.title: A third of babies have peanut allergy diagnosis removed
item.description: A world-first national program has discovered more than a third of babies thought to have a peanut allergy could safely have the diagnosis removed. And the findings are changing how Australia's health care system approaches infant food allergies.

item.title: Consuming colorful produce may help reduce COPD-related inflammation, flare-ups
item.description: Eating a diet rich in red, yellow and orange fruits and vegetables may help reduce inflammation and exacerbations associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), according to a new study in the September 2026 issue of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases: Journal of the COPD Foundation.

item.title: Age may influence links between psychedelic use and mental health
item.description: Age could play an important role in how psychedelic use relates to mental health, according to new research from the Department of Psychology at Durham University. Researchers found that adults with a history of using classic psychedelics, such as psilocybin (magic mushrooms) and LSD, reported lower levels of anxiety and depression than nonusers, but only in younger age groups. The associations became weaker with increasing age and were no longer evident among older adults.

item.title: How neurons in the hippocampus separate different aspects of experiences
item.description: When remembering an experience, people often recall not just where it happened, but also its timing and how it unfolded over time. This helps them to recall sequences of events and associations that can guide their actions in new scenarios.

item.title: Hypnotherapy and mindfulness reduce pain and anxiety for children with cancer
item.description: Psychosocial interventions can significantly reduce pain and anxiety for children undergoing cancer treatment, new Griffith University research has found. Dr. Karin Plummer from Griffith's School of Nursing and Midwifery investigated the efficacy of hypnosis, distraction techniques, virtual reality and mindfulness for children experiencing cancer pain.

item.title: Walking more shows sharper links to lower health care costs as adults age
item.description: More than 60 years after "I look up as I walk," known worldwide as "Sukiyaki," became Japan's most famous song about walking, a new study finds that as walkers look up, their predicted health care costs come down. In addition, how steeply the costs descend changes dramatically with age.

item.title: Study establishes weekly 'dose-of-nature' benchmarks for mental health benefits
item.description: A new study led by researchers at The University of Hong Kong (HKU) has established the first systematic weekly benchmarks for green space exposure and mental health. Drawing on 45 years of global research, the study reveals that even modest weekly contact with nature yields significant mental health benefits, with positive effects rising rapidly at lower levels of exposure before tapering off as visits become more frequent or prolonged.

item.title: Study links historic redlining to higher opioid overdose death rates in lower-graded neighborhoods
item.description: A new study from researchers at Boston Medical Center (BMC) found that Massachusetts neighborhoods given the lowest grades on historic redlining maps had 86% higher annual opioid-related overdose death rates than those given the highest grades. The study, published in the Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved, suggests that the long-term effects of historical disinvestment continue to affect health outcomes based on where people live.

item.title: Shorter days and dark afternoons can trigger depression. Here's how to fight back
item.description: As winter approaches and daylight hours grow shorter, people prone to seasonal depression can feel it in their bodies and brains.

item.title: Could an herbal supplement help you stop binge drinking?
item.description: An herbal supplement made from kudzu, a plant long used in traditional medicine from East Asia, may offer a new way to help people cut back on binge drinking, according to a UC San Francisco study.
